subject: Everyday Science
q: Malaria, polio, dengue fever and influenza are examples of:
explanation: All four are caused by pathogens (a protozoan or viruses) that can pass from one person to another, directly or through vectors.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Malaria is caused by a:
explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a single-celled protozoan that multiplies in the liver and red blood cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Malaria is spread by the bite of the female:
explanation: Only female Anopheles mosquitoes feed on blood and pass the Plasmodium parasite from one person to another.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dengue fever is transmitted mainly by the:
explanation: Aedes aegypti, which bites mostly during the day and breeds in clean standing water, carries the dengue virus.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dengue fever is caused by a:
explanation: Dengue is a viral disease, so antibiotics do not cure it; treatment focuses on fluids and monitoring platelets.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Tuberculosis is caused by a:
explanation: TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mainly affects the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The BCG vaccine protects against:
explanation: BCG (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin) is given to infants to protect against severe forms of tuberculosis.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Polio mainly affects the:
explanation: The poliovirus can attack nerve cells of the spinal cord, causing paralysis, usually of the legs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cholera spreads mainly through:
o: Touching the skin of a patient
explanation: Cholera bacteria are passed in faeces and spread where sewage contaminates drinking water or food.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) is given to patients with diarrhoea mainly to:
o: Kill the germs causing the diarrhoea
explanation: Dehydration is the main danger in diarrhoea; ORS, a mixture of salts and glucose in water, restores fluid balance.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Typhoid fever is caused by:
explanation: The bacterium Salmonella Typhi spreads through food and water contaminated with faeces.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hepatitis is an inflammation of the:
explanation: "Hepat-" refers to the liver; hepatitis is most often caused by hepatitis viruses.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hepatitis B and C are commonly spread through:
explanation: Both viruses are blood-borne; unsafe injections, unscreened transfusions and reused instruments are major routes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which types of viral hepatitis spread mainly through contaminated food and water?
explanation: Hepatitis A and E viruses pass through the faecal–oral route; B, C and D spread through blood and body fluids.

subject: Everyday Science
q: HIV weakens the body by attacking the:
explanation: HIV destroys helper T lymphocytes, leaving the body open to infections; the advanced stage is called AIDS.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Measles is caused by a:
explanation: Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that can be prevented by the measles (MMR) vaccine.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ringworm is a skin infection caused by a:
explanation: Despite its name, ringworm is a fungal infection that produces ring-shaped, itchy patches on the skin.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Rabies is usually transmitted to humans through:
o: The bite of an infected animal
explanation: The rabies virus is in the saliva of infected animals, mostly dogs, and enters through bites or scratches.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Tetanus bacteria usually enter the body through:
o: Deep wounds contaminated with soil or dirt
explanation: Spores of Clostridium tetani live in soil and dust and enter through wounds such as those from rusty nails.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cutaneous leishmaniasis, which occurs in parts of Pakistan, is spread by the:
explanation: The Leishmania parasite is transmitted by the bite of infected female sandflies and causes skin sores.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever ("Congo virus") is spread to humans mainly by:
o: Tick bites and contact with infected animal blood
explanation: The virus lives in ticks on livestock; people are infected by tick bites or by handling blood of infected animals, for example during slaughter.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Plague is spread to humans mainly by:
explanation: The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis lives in rodents and passes to humans through bites of their fleas.

subject: Everyday Science
q: COVID-19 is caused by a:
explanation: COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus spread mainly through respiratory droplets and aerosols.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections?
o: Viruses live only outside the body
Viruses are protected by the skin
Viruses are too large for antibiotics
Viruses lack the cell structures that antibiotics attack
explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial features such as cell walls and bacterial ribosomes; viruses have none of these and multiply inside our own cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Penicillin was discovered by:
explanation: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that the mould Penicillium killed bacteria around it, leading to the first antibiotic.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The first vaccine, against smallpox, was developed by:
explanation: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that inoculation with cowpox protected people from smallpox.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The bacterium that causes tuberculosis was identified in 1882 by:
explanation: Robert Koch discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a landmark in establishing that specific germs cause specific diseases.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The only human disease that has been eradicated worldwide is:
explanation: A global vaccination campaign led the WHO to declare smallpox eradicated in 1980.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A vaccine protects the body by:
o: Training the immune system to recognise a germ
Killing all germs already in the body
explanation: A vaccine exposes the immune system to a harmless form or part of a germ, so memory cells respond quickly to a real infection.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which practice is a major cause of antibiotic resistance?
o: Taking antibiotics unnecessarily or not finishing the course
explanation: Misuse lets the hardiest bacteria survive and multiply, producing strains that antibiotics no longer kill.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When most of a population is vaccinated, even unvaccinated people are protected because the germ cannot spread easily. This is called:
explanation: With few susceptible people, chains of transmission break, indirectly protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Antibodies passed from a mother to her baby through breast milk give the baby:
explanation: The baby receives ready-made antibodies rather than making its own, so the protection is passive and temporary.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Diabetes mellitus is a condition in which:
o: The blood has too few red cells
The blood glucose level stays too high
explanation: In diabetes the body makes too little insulin or cannot use it properly, so glucose builds up in the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A heart attack usually occurs when:
o: The heart valves become too large
Blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked
explanation: A blockage in a coronary artery, often a clot on fatty deposits, starves part of the heart muscle of oxygen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A stroke occurs when the blood supply is interrupted to part of the:
explanation: Without blood, brain cells are deprived of oxygen and begin to die, causing weakness, speech problems or paralysis.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cancer is best described as:
o: A bacterial infection of the blood
explanation: Cancer cells ignore normal controls on growth, forming tumours that can invade tissues and spread.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The addictive substance in tobacco is:
explanation: Nicotine causes dependence; tar and carbon monoxide in the smoke are harmful but not the addictive agent.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Asthma is a disease of the:
explanation: In asthma the airways become inflamed and narrowed, causing wheezing and breathlessness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the:
explanation: In pneumonia the alveoli fill with fluid or pus, making breathing difficult; it may be bacterial or viral.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Haemophilia is an inherited disorder in which:
explanation: People with haemophilia lack a clotting factor, so even small injuries can cause prolonged bleeding.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Thalassaemia is an inherited blood disorder that affects the production of:
explanation: Faulty genes reduce haemoglobin production, causing anaemia; thalassaemia major needs regular transfusions.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The recommended first aid for a minor burn is to:
o: Hold it under cool running water for several minutes
explanation: Cool water removes heat and limits tissue damage; butter traps heat, and ice or burst blisters worsen injury and infection risk.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In first aid for a nosebleed, the person should:
o: Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
explanation: Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat, and pressure on the soft part of the nose helps a clot form.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The first step in controlling heavy bleeding from a wound is to:
o: Give the person something to eat
Apply firm direct pressure on the wound
Wash the wound with hot water
explanation: Direct pressure compresses damaged vessels and helps clotting; removing clots restarts bleeding.

subject: Everyday Science
q: CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) is given to a person who:
o: Is not breathing and has no effective heartbeat
explanation: Chest compressions and rescue breaths keep oxygenated blood reaching the brain until the heart can be restarted.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In first aid, a suspected broken limb should be:
explanation: Immobilising the limb prevents further damage to bone ends, vessels and nerves until medical help arrives.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Correct first aid for a snake bite includes:
o: Giving the victim a hot drink
Cutting the wound and sucking out the venom
Tying a tight wire above the bite
Keeping the victim calm and the bitten limb still
explanation: Keeping still slows the spread of venom while the victim is taken to hospital for antivenom; cutting and sucking cause harm.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A person suffering from heatstroke should first be:
o: Moved to a cool place and cooled down
explanation: Heatstroke is a dangerous rise in body temperature; rapid cooling is the priority while medical help is sought.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Influenza spreads from person to person mainly through:
explanation: The flu virus is carried in respiratory droplets, which is why covering coughs and washing hands reduce spread.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Washing hands with soap helps prevent disease mainly because it:
explanation: Soap lifts dirt and microbes off the skin so they are rinsed away, breaking the route by which many infections spread.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A disease outbreak that spreads across many countries and continents is called a:
explanation: An epidemic is confined to a region; when it spreads worldwide, as COVID-19 did, it becomes a pandemic.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A disease that is constantly present in a particular area is described as:
explanation: Endemic diseases, like malaria in some regions, occur at a steady expected level in a population.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Diseases that spread from animals to humans are called:
explanation: Rabies, anthrax and Congo fever are zoonoses, passing from animals to people directly or through vectors.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The time between infection and the appearance of symptoms is called the:
explanation: During incubation the germ multiplies in the body before symptoms show; its length varies from disease to disease.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The DPT vaccine protects against diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and:
explanation: DPT is a combined vaccine given in infancy against three serious bacterial diseases.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The MMR vaccine protects against measles, mumps and:
explanation: MMR combines protection against three viral diseases; rubella (German measles) is dangerous in pregnancy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Mumps causes painful swelling of the:
explanation: The mumps virus typically inflames the parotid salivary glands, giving swollen cheeks and jaw.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Leprosy mainly affects the:
explanation: Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, damages skin and peripheral nerves, leading to loss of sensation.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice) is usually a sign of a problem with the:
explanation: Jaundice results from build-up of the yellow pigment bilirubin, which a healthy liver clears from the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Conjunctivitis is an inflammation of the:
explanation: Conjunctivitis ("pink eye") inflames the thin membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A cataract is a condition in which the eye's:
o: Optic nerve is damaged by pressure
explanation: Clouding of the lens blurs vision; it is common in old age and treated by replacing the lens surgically.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Osteoporosis is a condition in which:
explanation: Loss of bone mineral makes bones porous and fracture-prone; calcium, vitamin D and exercise help prevent it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Scabies, an intensely itchy skin condition, is caused by:
o: Tiny mites burrowing into the skin
explanation: The itch mite Sarcoptes scabiei burrows under the skin and spreads through close contact.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A drug that reduces fever is called an:
explanation: Antipyretics such as paracetamol lower body temperature; they do not kill the germs causing the fever.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A chemical applied to a wound on the skin to kill germs is an:
explanation: Antiseptics such as dilute iodine or chlorhexidine are safe on living tissue; disinfectants are for surfaces.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Antacids relieve acidity because they:
explanation: Antacids are mild bases, such as magnesium hydroxide, that react with and neutralise hydrochloric acid.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An ECG records the:
explanation: An electrocardiogram traces the heart's electrical signals and helps detect irregular rhythms and heart attacks.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated from a person's:
explanation: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres, a rough screen for under- or overweight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Removing stagnant water around homes helps control dengue because it:
o: Destroys the breeding sites of mosquitoes
Kills the dengue virus in patients
explanation: Aedes mosquitoes lay eggs in standing water in pots, tyres and coolers; removing it cuts the mosquito population.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous to humans because it:
o: Destroys the lining of the stomach
Binds to haemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport
explanation: Carbon monoxide attaches to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, starving the tissues of oxygen.
